notes.text: The heart — There is nothing so false and deceitful as the heart of man; deceitful in its apprehensions of things, in the hopes and promises which it nourishes, in the assurances that it gives us; unsearchable by others, deceitful with reference to ourselves, and abominably wicked, so that neither can a man know his own heart, nor can any other know that of his neighbour's.

glossa.text: *Cursed be the man. ((ID.))* Cursed therefore be Paul of Samosata and Photinus, who although a holy, etc., *as far as* that both might become one, and that we should adore not the creature, but the Creator.

*Blessed be the man,* etc. ((ID.)) As if to say: Cursed are the Jews, and the heretics, who have not hope in the Lord, etc., *as far as* who once died for us, and dies no more: and he says, *I am the life ((Joan. XIV))*.
*Which sendeth forth its roots toward moisture. ((ID.))* As if he should say: from the Jewish dryness he passes over to the grace of baptism.

notes.text: Blessed — The Hebrew words are very emphatical: O the blessedness of that man! Counsel - That doth not lead his life according to their counsel, or manner of living. Standeth - Which notes a more settled abode in it. Way - In their manner of conversation. Seat - Which notes a constant and resolved perseverance in their wicked courses. Scornful - Of those who make a mock of sin, and scoff at goodness and goodmen. Divers observe a gradation in this verse; the following clause still exceeding the former, for standing is more than walking, and sitting more than standing; and sinners in scripture use, are worse than the ungodly, and the scornful are the worst of sinners.
Day and night — Not seldom and slightly, but diligently, and constantly.
Whither — His happiness is not short and transitory, but, like those trees which are continually green and flourishing.
Ungodly — Their condition is far different. Chaff - They are restless and unquiet: their seeming felicity, hath no firm foundation, but quickly vanishes and flees away as chaff before the wind.
Not stand — Not endure the trial. Judgment - In the great and general judgment of the world.

Knoweth — He approves, loves, and delights in them, and therefore will recompence them. Perish - All their designs and courses shall come to nothing, and they shall perish with them. There is nothing in this psalm which is not applicable to Christ, but some things which are not all applicable to David. Threatenings denounced against the adversaries of Christ's kingdom, ver. 1-6. Promises made to Christ, ver. 7-9. Counsel given to all, to submit to him, ver. 10-12.

glossa.text: « Blessed is the man who hath not gone away, etc. » ((AUG., Enarr. in Psal., tom. III.)) The order, Adam went away when he withdrew from God; he stood, when he was delighted with sin; he sat, when, confirmed in pride, he could not return, save as set free by this man, who had none of these things. Adam went away when he consented to the persuasion of the devil; he stood, while he ate the apple; he sat, while he excused himself: « The woman whom thou gavest me seduced me. » ((Gen. III)) . After the likeness of exiles, who, while they are on the road, are more easily called back, while they now stand, with more difficulty: at length with the greatest difficulty, when they have there been made masters and lords. ((REMI.)) There is sinning by thought, by act, and by words in teaching. ((CASS.)) The impious man is so against God, the sinner against himself, the pestilent man against his neighbour. « In the chair, giving an example of sinning. » ((CASS.)) The throne is of kings, the tribunal of judges, the chair properly of teachers. ((Ibid.)) It is as though he said: You who have fallen through the first Adam, be ye conformed to this second one: because the blessed man is the contrary of the first

« But in the law. » AUG. ((CASS.)) Here he is shown full of every good in himself. ((AUG.)) It is not perfect praise to flee the things to be blamed, unless the things to be praised follow. In the order in which they grew in the first man, they are taken away in the second.

« In the law. » ((Ibid.)) He who is in the law acts according to the law, he who is under the law is acted upon according to the law: the one is free, the other a slave. ((Ibid. AMBR.)) One thing is the law which is written for him that serves, another that which is beheld with the mind by him who has no need of letters. « The will. » ((CASS.)) That there be no weariness of labour, nor idleness, but he shall meditate always. The will of sense is under the law; of reason, in the law; of divinity, above the law.

« And he shall be. » ((Ibid.)) Here he is shown useful to us, giving the fruit of life, and leaves, and overshadowing us, « Blessed is the man. But in the law. And he shall be. » The full definition of the blessed man. All these things belong not to every blessed man, but to Christ alone. « As a tree. » ((Ibid.)) After the likeness of the tree of life which is in paradise, whereof obedient man was to have eaten. « A tree. » ((Ibid.)) In paradise there is the tree of life, a tree unto life, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. « Of waters. » ((AUG.)) The waters are the Holy Spirit, according to that word: « He that shall have believed in me, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water ((Joan. VII)), » and it is against the heats of the vices. ((CASS.)) Or, by water, the wisdom of God, by which the inner man is restored, as thirst by water. ((AUG.)) Or the mortal race, as Job: « Many waters, many peoples, » because they flow down into death, as waters into the sea. « He shall give. » ((Ibid.)) To give pertains to the rational sense and to the will of the one offering. « And the leaf. » ((Ibid.)) As the leaves cover the fruit, so the words of the Lord guard his promises. « And all things. » ((Ibid.)) Why go through them one by one.

« Not so the impious. » Here by the vengeance upon the wicked he terrifies the adverse, the dread of these makes what has gone before more welcome. « From the face of the earth. » ((AUG.)) Of eternal stability, because as this earth nourishes and holds up a man, so that other earth holds up the inner man.

« Therefore they shall not rise again. » Because the wind casteth them away, that is, therefore, because they have been given over to a reprobate sense: therefore they do not rise again in the first resurrection, that they may judge themselves in counsel, that they may set the wills of God before their own. Or in the council, that is, in the harmonious multitude of the just, the impious idolaters, or apostates. Sinners, false Christians: or else therefore they do not rise again in the time to come, that they may judge, or that, being judged, they may rest in the council, that is, in the college of the just. « In judgment, etc. » In the judgment there will be four orders: some shall judge and shall not be judged, as the most perfect; some shall neither judge nor be judged, as the damned unbelievers; some shall be judged and shall be saved, as the moderately good; some shall be judged and shall perish, as the evil faithful. « In the council. » ((AUG.)) In the eternal good, to follow which was counsel to the saints. « Or in the council, » in the judgment, that they may judge together with them; for there is judgment when different sins are punished with different penalties; and it is said from this by likeness. « They rise again. » What resurrections these are: of the soul, from sins in the present; of the body, from death in the time to come, whereby it shall be made impassible and immortal.
« For the Lord knoweth, etc., » That is, these do not rise again in the soul, because God does not approve their works, but those of the just only.

notes.text: How say some — Who probably had been heathen philosophers.
If there be no resurrection — If it be a thing flatly impossible.
Then is our preaching — From a commission supposed to be given after the resurrection. Vain - Without any real foundation.
If the dead rise not — If the very notion of a resurrection be, as they say, absurd and impossible.

Ye are still in your sins — That is, under the guilt of them. So that there needed something more than reformation, (which was plainly wrought,) in order to their being delivered from the guilt of sin even that atonement, the sufficiency of which God attested by raising our great Surety from the grave.
They who sleep in Christ — Who have died for him, or believing in him. Are perished - Have lost their life and being together.

If in this life only we have hope — If we look for nothing beyond the grave. But if we have a divine evidence of things not seen, if we have "a hope full of immortality," if we now taste of "the powers of the world to come," and see "the crown that fadeth not away," then, notwithstanding" all our present trials, we are more happy than all men.

But now — St. Paul declares that Christians "have hope," not "in this life only." His proof of the resurrection lies in a narrow compass, ver. 12-19. Almost all the rest of the chapter is taken up in illustrating, vindicating, and applying it. The proof is short, but solid and convincing, that which arose from Christ's resurrection. Now this not only proved a resurrection possible, but, as it proved him to be a divine teacher, proved the certainty of a general resurrection, which he so expressly taught. The first fruit of them that slept - The earnest, pledge, and insurance of their resurrection who slept in him: even of all the righteous. It is of the resurrection of these, and these only, that the apostle speaks throughout the chapter.

glossa.text: *But if Christ.* Thus far he has shown that Christ rose again. Now by his resurrection he proves the resurrection of the dead. The false apostles were denying that Christ had truly suffered, or been buried, or risen again, or come in the flesh.

*But we are found.* These things and others are brought in for this cause, that the Corinthians may blush who follow the error of the false apostles, an error on which these absurdities follow, which he himself also condemns. Therefore, lest they remain in this error, he says: *I have found,* etc. *Inveni*; read *Invenimur*, "we are found" *Against God.* Not by a lesser, but perhaps by a greater wickedness is falsehood praised in God than truth is blamed.

*And if Christ be not,* etc. If Christ has not risen again; Christ is held in death. And if in death, then also in sin, which is the cause of death And if he is held in sin, he could not remit your sins. And so you are still in your sins, which you believed had been forgiven you, and so your faith is vain.

notes.text: On a plain — At the foot of the mountain.

In the following verses our Lord, in the audience of his newly- chosen disciples, and of the multitude, repeats, standing on the plain, many remarkable passages of the sermon he had before delivered, sitting on the mount. He here again pronounces the poor and the hungry, the mourners, and the persecuted, happy; and represents as miserable those who are rich, and full, and joyous, and applauded: because generally prosperity is a sweet poison, and affliction a healing, though bitter medicine. Let the thought reconcile us to adversity, and awaken our caution when the world smiles upon us; when a plentiful table is spread before us, and our cup is running over; when our spirits are gay; and we hear (what nature loves) our own praise from men. Happy are ye poor — The word seems here to be taken literally: ye who have left all for me. Matt. v, 3.
Miserable are ye rich — If ye have received or sought your consolation or happiness therein.
Full — Of meat and drink, and worldly goods. That laugh - That are of a light trifling spirit.
Woe to you when all men shall speak well of you — But who will believe this?

glossa.text:
*And coming down,* etc. The Lord, about to choose apostles, went up into the mountains; about to teach the crowds, he returns to the plains, because the crowds are not able to see Christ except in what is lowly, and rarely is it found either that a crowd follows the Lord to higher things, or that any weak man is cured on the mountain; but when the fever of lusts has been quenched and the light of knowledge kindled, each one step by step goes up to the height of the virtues.

*The sea coast.* Not from the neighbouring sea of Galilee, because they do not set this in the place of the miracle, but it is named from the great sea. In which Tyre and Sidon also could be comprehended. But because they are cities of the Gentiles, they are deliberately set down by name, that it may be intimated how great is the power of Christ, which stirs even foreign cities.

*That they might hear.* If we say that there are two discourses, he went up into the mountain, and had his disciples there; and afterwards he came down and made this one to the crowd. If we say there was one, it must be understood thus, that he went up into the mountain, and after a little came down, and there made the discourse, where there was a level place.
*To touch him.* He touches Christ who faithfully believes in him. He is touched by Christ who is made firm in him. He who so touches and is touched is healed by the power of his spirit.

*And he, lifting up,* etc. Although he speaks generally to all, he lifts his eyes specially upon the disciples, that they who receive the word of God with the intent ear of the heart may more widely receive the light of the inward savour; to whom, sitting on the mountain, he opens his mouth, that he may utter great things upon them; standing on the plain he directs his eyes, that they may patiently understand what they hear. *Blessed are the poor,* etc. They who cannot yet climb the citadel of consummated virtue are meanwhile to be cherished with the beatitude of a general perfection, that little by little advancing to better things, while they gladly listen to the Lord standing on the plain, they may at some time loftily ascend to him sitting on the mountain. For those upon whose hearts he still presses to tame them, these he addresses as it were standing. Those whom he finds exercised by long endeavour and now teachable, to these he imparts mystical things as one resting at ease.

((BEDA.)) What in Matthew is fully said by eight beatitudes in the sermon of perfection to the apostles on the top of the mountain, this in Luke, etc., *as far as* but because he excelled in faith, by faith he deserved the primacy before the rest.

*You that now hunger.* He who hungers has compassion on him that hungers: by compassion he gives freely, by giving freely he becomes just; he makes himself equal to his inferiors, he shuts out guile, he seeks the truth. *You that now weep.* He who for the riches of Christ's inheritance, for the bread of eternal life, for the hope of heavenly joys, desires weeping, hunger and poverty, is blessed; much more blessed he who does not fear to keep these virtues amid adversities.

*Rejoice and be glad.* Amid the hatreds of hearts, amid the reproaches of tongues, amid the hands of persecutors, be conversant with a gladder heart, in view of the reward on high. *For according to these things.* By the example of the prophets he strengthens them, because those who speak the truth are wont to suffer persecution.

*But woe,* etc. Matthew on the mountain describes only the beatitudes of the upright; but Luke on the plain describes also the woe of the wicked, because hearers still untrained are to be driven to good things by threats and terrors, while for the perfect it is enough to be invited by rewards. *But woe.* Since above the kingdom of heaven is said to be the poor's, it appears by the contrary that he estranges himself from this kingdom who seeks his consolation in temporal things. Nor are riches so much in fault as the love of riches.

Mystically: the rich man is the Jewish people, or the heretic, or the philosopher of the world, who, delighted with the abundance of words and the patronage of eloquence, having gone beyond the simplicity of the true faith, have laid up useless treasures, disputing according to the usage of the world about the generation of Christ; who in the world to come shall recognize the neediness of their faith, and, wasted with eternal fasting, shall know that the food of faithlessness which they belch forth in the present is the cause of so great a punishment. And there shall be a time when they shall bewail their laughter. To whom it is well said: *Woe, when men shall bless you;* because while here they please the powerful, they subject themselves to a perpetual curse, because as the poor, the hungry, the weeping are proved by the wickedness of the evil, so those given to riches, to feasts and to laughter, by the evil retinue of those who fawn upon them, are cherished unto a greater punishment.

*You that are filled,* etc. You who among the rich abound the more, like the rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen and with feasts, who seeks a drop of water from Lazarus' finger.

*Woe to you that now laugh,* etc. Solomon: *The heart of the wise man is where there is sadness, the heart of fools where there is gladness ((Eccl. VII))*; teaching that folly is to be ascribed to those who laugh, prudence to those who weep.
*Shall bless you,* etc. A great part of the punishment of sinners is that their crimes are not only not reproved, but are moreover praised as though well done.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Happy are those who delight in the law of the Lord.
Blessed are those who trust in God.
They are like trees planted by streams of water.
Blessed are those who trust in God.
Blessed are you who are poor, who hunger, who weep.
Come, let us worship. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Imagine a tree by a river — roots deep, leaves green even in the dry season, unafraid of heat.
Blessed are those who trust in the Lord.
That is the life rooted in God; not anxious, not withered, but bearing fruit in its time.
Blessed are those who trust in the Lord.
And the blessings come to the unlikely: the poor, the hungry, the grieving, the cast out.
Blessed are those who trust in the Lord.
So sink your roots by the water; the world's scorekeeping is not the kingdom's.
Blessed are those who trust in the Lord; they shall not fear!
